bib.title: AI & Human Co-Improvement for Safer Co-Superintelligence

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AI & Human Co-Improvement for Safer Co-Superintelligence" (running head "Self-Improving AI"), Jason Weston and Jakob Foerster, FAIR at Meta. arXiv 2512.05356v2 [cs.AI], 14 Dec 2025. It is a position paper and was not peer reviewed.

COVERAGE: All 34,100 of 34,100 chars read, covering pages 1-9. The body runs to page 5, then the acknowledgements and references (skimmed for origins). There are no appendices and no results tables. The extraction is clean, apart from a garbled title and header on page 1. I did not run the figure-caption script. The only figure, on page 2, has no numbered caption in the text, and its explanatory text is quoted below.

CLAIMS (ranked; the paper contains no measured numbers)

- **Central position.** Autonomous self-improvement is neither the fastest nor the safest route to superintelligence. Keeping humans in the research loop is better on both counts.
  - number: none
  - setup: a position argument about AI-research loops, with no experiments
  - quote: "We have argued that the existing goal of autonomous self-improving AI is misguided for two reasons: it is not the fastest way to achieve superintelligence, nor the safest."
  - where: p.4, Conclusion

- **Definition of the two loop shapes.** In self-improvement the human builds a seed and then leaves the loop. In co-improvement the human builds the first system and then collaborates with the AI on every later improvement.
  - number: none
  - setup: the page-2 figure, with Seed, Improvement and Improvement nodes
  - quote: "In self-improving AI, humans build an AI that improves itself autonomously with no human in the loop. In co-improvement humans build the first system, but then collaborate with the AI for further improvement, so both humans and AI get the benefit."
  - where: p.2, figure caption text

- **Human involvement at each step is the safety lever.** Human involvement at every step gives more chances to steer, and more transparency and steerability. An autonomous system risks goal misspecification.
  - number: none
  - setup: an argued expectation, not tested
  - quote: "when humans are working with the AI system to help achieve this at each step of the loop, we have more opportunities to guide this process towards positive benefits to humanity."
  - also: "an entirely autonomous AI self-improvement system can suffer from goal misspecification (e.g. what it means to "solve AI" does not take human needs into account)."
  - where: p.2 (What can we gain?), p.3 (From co-improvement to co-superintelligence)

- **Optimise research quality, not artifact throughput.** The goal is better research, not faster production of artifacts such as papers by full automation.
  - number: none
  - setup: contrasted with end-to-end AI-scientist systems (Lu et al. 2024, Nathani et al. 2025)
  - quote: "Crucially, in contrast to recent end-to-end AI scientist approaches [11, 15] the goal is to improve research quality, rather than to accelerate research artifact production (such as papers) via full automation."
  - where: p.3

- **The human share of work is expected to shift over time.** It is not fixed, and the paper does not set levels or thresholds.
  - number: none
  - setup: forward-looking expectation
  - quote: "While today most of the AI research is done by humans, we expect over time the burden will become more shared – as AI improves it can work with us to take more of the workload in providing solutions."
  - where: p.1

- **Collaboration skill should be targeted and benchmarked, like coding.** Collaboration skills improve when targeted, as coding did. The authors propose benchmarks and training data for research collaboration.
  - number: none
  - setup: argument by analogy with coding, with no data
  - quote: "That is, measuring the research collaboration skills of AI with new benchmarks, and constructing training data and methods that improve these benchmarks" (the extraction reads: "that means measuring the research collaboration skills of AI with new benchmarks, and constructing training data and methods that improve these benchmarks, much as we do with building other skills.")
  - where: p.2

- **Table 1 lists ten research-pipeline stages for human-AI collaboration.**
  - number: none
  - setup: a taxonomy
  - stages: problem identification, benchmark creation, method innovation, joint experiment design, collaborative execution, evaluation and error analysis, safety and alignment, systems and infrastructure co-design, real-world integration, scientific communication, collective intelligence, and bidirectional co-improvement (Table 1 lists twelve rows in total).
  - quote: "Evaluation & error analysis ... Analyzing performance both on benchmarks and individual cases for successes & failures (at scale via AI); feedback loop for research iteration."
  - where: p.3, Table 1

- **Table 2 maps self-improvement mechanisms to the axes they change, with open issues.** The axes are parameters, train data, objective, architecture and overall code. The open issues include reward hacking and unvalidated self-judgment. Rows are classic parameter optimization, self-training, self-challenging and synthetic data, self-evaluation and self-reward, algorithm or architecture self-modification, recursive self-improvement, and metaphorical usage.
  - number: none (the table uses filled-dot counts, not data)
  - quote: "can drift away from human reasoning without strong priors" and "reward hacking" (self-training row)
  - also: "validating reliability of self-generated judgments" (self-evaluation row)
  - where: p.3, Table 2

- **Autonomy removes chances for human intervention.** The paper quotes Silver and Sutton, who concede that experience-driven autonomy leaves humans fewer chances to intervene.
  - number: none
  - quote: "provides fewer opportunities for humans to intervene and mediate the agent's actions, and therefore requires a high bar of trust and responsibility"
  - where: p.5, Contrasting Positions (quoting [65])

- **Self-improvement building blocks are already standard.** LLM-as-a-Judge and synthetic data creation are already standard building blocks for frontier models. Self-improvement of architecture and code is still "in its infancy".
  - number: none
  - quote: "approaches like synthetic data creation and LLM-as-a-Judge are now standard building blocks for frontier models. The quest for AI that improves its own architectures and rewrites its own code is still in its infancy"
  - where: p.1

- **Safety work should run now, not be added after deployment.**
  - number: none
  - quote: "we believe this research should be in progress now – not added on later when systems are fully deployed and it is too late."
  - where: p.4

LIMITS
- It is a position paper. It has no experiments, no ablations, no measured comparison of co-improvement against self-improvement, and no numbers. "Faster" and "safer" are asserted, not shown.
- It gives no concrete protocol for human checkpoints and no loop design. It never says what a human does at which step, how much oversight is enough, or how oversight scales.
- The authors concede that it is optimistic ("This optimistic viewpoint contends ... if done correctly"). They also concede that AI will outpace humans in more dimensions over time.
- The paper does not address the human-bottleneck or cost objection. It does not explain how humans stay useful as AI capability grows.
- It is scoped to AI-research loops at frontier labs, not to engineering loops such as coding agents.
- The authors are at Meta FAIR, and several self-citations (Self-Rewarding, Self-Challenging, SPICE, Self-Instruct) show a stake in this area.

BUILDS ON
- Self-improvement lineage: Schmidhuber 2007 (Gödel machines), Silver and Sutton 2025 (era of experience), Clune 2019 (AI-GAs), Silver et al. 2021 (Reward is enough), and Bostrom.
- Practical self-improvement: Wang et al. 2022 (Self-Instruct), Yuan et al. 2024 (Self-Rewarding), Bai et al. 2022 (Constitutional AI), Zhao et al. 2025 (Absolute Zero), Zhou et al. 2025 (Self-Challenging), Novikov et al. 2025 (AlphaEvolve), and Lu et al. 2024 (AI Scientist).
- Human-centred and oversight positions: Shneiderman 2022, Dafoe et al. 2021 (Cooperative AI), Bowman et al. 2022 (scalable oversight), Gottweis et al. 2025 (AI co-scientist), Russell 2022, and Bengio 2025.

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Page 2 figure, which has no numbered caption in the extraction. It shows a Seed node with Improvement arrows. Self-improvement is a closed autonomous loop. Co-improvement is a loop with humans and AI both inside it.
- It is a quick visual for loop shapes: autonomous versus human-in-the-loop.
- Table 1 (p.3) lists the collaboration stages. Table 2 (p.3) maps self-improvement mechanisms to open issues.

PLACEMENT
- **Primary: 07 autonomy ladder.** Use it as a citation for the end-state contrast, with fully autonomous self-improvement at one extreme and human-in-the-loop co-improvement at the other. The paper gives no rungs, so it can only frame the endpoints, and a one-line cite is enough. Quote: "In co-improvement humans build the first system, but then collaborate with the AI for further improvement".
- **Secondary: 08 self-improving loops.** Add a sharpens citation and a references row, with one sentence at most, because 08 is over length. The sentence would say that Table 2 lists the self-improvement axes and their open issues (reward hacking, unvalidated self-judgment) and that the paper argues for keeping humans in the loop. Do not add new prose beyond that.
- **Optional: 09 failure modes.** The line about drift from human reasoning and reward hacking in self-training could be cited there. It is a weak source, because it lists issues without evidence.
- **Not for 02, 03 or 05.** It offers no loop shape mechanics, scorekeeper or long-running design.
- **Overall:** only partly on-topic. It is conceptual and position-level, and it gives no evidence for any number or mechanism in the course. Cite it as a framing source and never as an empirical claim. Its only contribution that bears on loop design is the human-in-loop versus autonomous contrast.

PROBLEMS: The page-1 title and header are garbled by decorative glyphs. The text contains no embedded instructions. Reference [14] has a mangled author name ("EstapÃŠ"), which is harmless.
